transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-15
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Reeves (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Tempest VP Eng), Sara Ortiz (Platform Lead), Imran Malik (Security Architect)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
Tempest asked about reserved node sizing, how Redwood Dedicated handles isolation and tenant fencing, options for VPC peering vs private control plane, KMS integration, and fallback to hosted variants during surge. Agreed to run a benchmark with sample traffic and share compliance docs.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh, Marcus, Sara, Imran, can you hear us ok?
[00:05] Marcus: Yep, loud and clear. Good to meet you all.
[00:09] Jordan: Awesome. Quick intros — Jordan Reeves here, AE on the Redwood Dedicated team. Priya's our SE who will own the technical bench and run through the VPC bits.
[00:16] Priya: Hi all. I'll be the hands-on person for the evals — happy to dive into topology and perf.
[00:21] Sara: Sara, Platform Lead at Tempest. We're looking at options for predictable inference costs and low tail latency for our real-time summarization API.
[00:29] Imran: Imran, Security. I mainly want to cover encryption, key management, audit logs, and any multi-tenant blast radius concerns.
[00:36] Jordan: Perfect. Goal for today — understand your traffic and success criteria, align on Dedicated vs Private, and agree next steps: benchmarks and compliance artifacts.

[00:44] Marcus: High level — we have a production svc that does short-form summarization. Baseline is about 200k tokens/day currently, but we expect microsurges up to 700k tokens for new feature rollouts. Peak RPS is about 400 for 2–5 minute windows during internal experiments.
[01:02] Priya: Okay that helps. Are those bursts correlated to a small number of users or wide fanout?
[01:07] Marcus: Mostly a fanout from our webhooks — so many lightweight requests, each short. Latency target is 200–350ms 95th. Cost target is to keep per-token costs under a threshold — we can't triple op-ex overnight.
[01:20] Sara: Also we have compliance constraints: PII redaction pipeline upstream, and we can't allow any token material to be logged externally for retention >30 days.
[01:30] Imran: To add — we require KMS integration, customer-managed keys if possible. And audit logs for every request with trace ids. SOC 2 compliance required.
[01:38] Jordan: Great, this is the typical Dedicated vs Hosted decision — Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools and predictable throughput, with network isolation via VPC peering or private control plane. Hosted is faster to spin up but harder to meet the audit/KMS constraints.
[01:51] Marcus: Can Dedicated be in our VPC? We're cloud-first and want to avoid NAT hops if possible.
[01:56] Priya: Two options — VPC peering with a private peered endpoint, or Redwood Private where the control plane is customer-managed in your VPC. Peering is quicker; Private is for air-gapped or strict data residency. There's also a hybrid where inference nodes are in a private subnet with peering.
[02:15] Imran: If we do peering, where are the KMS keys? We need CMK (customer-managed key) support and HSM-backed options.
[02:22] Jordan: Redwood supports KMS integration — you can bring your CMK in major cloud providers, and for on-prem/HSMs there are options in Private deployments. Logs can be exported to your SIEM.
[02:31] Sara: Good. On fallback — if our Dedicated pool is saturated during a burst, what's the fallback? Auto-scale? Or do we get queued?
[02:39] Priya: There are configurable policies. For Reserved capacity you can define burst window and hot-pool warm nodes. We also provide graceful fallback to compatible hosted model variants with policy rules — e.g., fall back to an 8-bit quantized variant with slightly higher latency but lower cost, or route to a shared hosted tier for non-sensitive traffic.
[02:58] Marcus: Hmm. That fallback to hosted — does that mean tokens might leave our VPC? That's a hard no for certain traffic.
[03:05] Imran: Yes we need to keep sensitive traffic inside the peered network. Some customers split traffic — sensitive requests required on Dedicated; non-sensitive can hit hosted fallback.
[03:15] Jordan: Exactly. Priya, can you sketch out policy options?
[03:18] Priya: Sure. Option A: Strict isolation — no external fallback; instead we provide surge buffer (hot pool) sized to X hours of burst, plus prewarm. Option B: Partial fallback — traffic marked as non-sensitive can route to hosted fallback. Option C: Private deployment — control plane inside your VPC, so even fallback stays within your network depending on topology. Each has cost/ops tradeoffs.
[03:40] Marcus: What's the warm pool sizing thought process? We need an example formula.
[03:44] Priya: We typically look at historical burst probability and latency SLO. E.g., for 500 RPS peaks lasting 5 minutes with 95th latency 300ms, you'd need ~N GPUs prewarmed (depends on model token per inference). We can run a simulation once we have token distribution.
[03:58] Marcus: We'll share our 7-day histogram.
[04:00] Imran: On encryption at rest and in transit — can we keep TLS endpoints inside our VPC and use our certs?
[04:06] Jordan: Mutual TLS and VPC endpoints are supported. For certs, we usually manage TLS on the redirect endpoint; there are ways to terminate in your network with Private.
[04:16] Sara: On observability — we need per-request latency and token-level cost breakdown to feed our internal billing.
[04:22] Priya: The Redwood Console exports per-route cost and latency metrics. We can push logs to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver and provide token-level estimates. The accuracy is strong but not perfect — sometimes token accounting shifts with quantized models.
[04:36] Marcus: About model choices — is it possible to deploy a smaller quantized variant in the Dedicated pool for cost savings?
[04:42] Priya: Yes — Dedicated supports multiple model variants. You can pin versions, and we recommend a mix: baseline high-accuracy model for sensitive requests, and a lower-cost quantized variant for bulk inference. That also informs capacity planning.
[04:56] Marcus: If we pin versions, how are rollouts handled? Canary?
[04:59] Jordan: We support canary rollouts and traffic splitting in the deployment config. You can define automatic fallback if quality regresses.
[05:07] Imran: A couple of compliance specifics — we need immutable audit logs for 1 year, and access control via SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning. Also role-based access control for node ops.
[05:19] Jordan: That's standard for our enterprise plan. SSO/SAML + SCIM supported, RBAC for console and API keys, and logs can be sent to your log archive.
[05:28] Sara: What's the expected procurement/contract timeline? We're trying to align with a Q2 feature launch.
[05:33] Jordan: For Dedicated reserve there's typically a 3–6 week procurement + onboarding window depending on legal review. Private deployments can take longer (6–12 weeks) because of network and KMS integrations.
[05:44] Marcus: Budget — we need an order of magnitude for 2–4 reserved GPUs vs a hot pool with 10% buffer.
[05:51] Priya: I can run a sizing model once we have token distribution. As a rough example: a single A100-equivalent node can handle X throughput for model Y (this conversation often turns into a bunch of numbers), but rather than guessing I'll put numbers in the benchmark plan.
[06:05] Marcus: Sounds good. On the benchmark — we want a realistic test: our payloads are short, median token length ~40, but some long-chains at 400 tokens. Can Redwood simulate that mix?
[06:15] Priya: Absolutely. We'll create a synthetic load that mirrors your histogram and include cold-start patterns. We'll also test prewarm and warm-pool behavior.
[06:23] Jordan: One more piece — SLAs. What uptime/latency SLAs are available for Dedicated?
[06:29] Priya: We provide an SLA-backed uptime for Dedicated and latency targets for reserved capacity tiers. The exact numbers are in the enterprise SLA. We can include that in the contract.
[06:36] Imran: For data residency — we want all inference to run in us-west-2. Can Dedicated be pinned to region?
[06:41] Jordan: Yes, you can pin region. For Private, you manage the control plane region.
[06:45] Sara: Ok, next steps recap?
[06:47] Jordan: We'll do a benchmark with the sample traffic, share pricing and contract draft, and provide SOC2/ISO artifacts and an architecture doc. Tempest will share traffic histograms and a list of sensitive routes.
[06:58] Marcus: We'll also identify which routes are allowed to fall back to hosted, and which must remain in Dedicated.
[07:03] Imran: I'll send the KMS requirements and current SIEM ingestion pattern.
[07:08] Priya: I'll follow up with the benchmark plan and propose dates for the run.
[07:12] Jordan: Great. Any final questions?
[07:15] Marcus: Two quick asks — can we get an example contract with pre-emptible protections in the reserve wording? And do you offer burst credits?
[07:24] Jordan: We can include guardrails in the contract around eviction tolerance and preemption. Burst credits are something we can discuss — often modeled as hot-pool hours. I'll propose a few options in the pricing deck.
[07:36] Sara: Thanks, everyone. This was productive.
[07:39] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up by EOD Friday with the deck and calendar invite for the bench.

[07:45] -- End of recorded transcript --
